title: Two Gregorys and a friendship
hookLine: Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil, friends since student days

cards: Athens, a city full of schools, and full of students who like to make newcomers miserable. Two young men from Cappadocia are there to study. One is Basil.
The other is Gregory, whose family was from Nazianzus. Gregory, by his own account, stepped in to spare Basil the usual treatment new arrivals got. A favor between students.
It turned into the friendship of their lives. And there's a second Gregory in this story too.

teach.b: First, how Gregory describes it. After Basil died, Gregory gave a long speech in his honor, and that speech is where we hear about Athens. He says the two of them shared everything: lodgings, meals, studies, hopes.
They seemed, he says, to have one soul living in two bodies. Second, the two roads.

A great city has endless distractions, and Gregory says they knew only two roads: one to the churches and the teachers there, the other to their lessons. Feasts, shows and parties they left to others.
Their friendship had a direction, and it was the same direction. Third, the crack. This friendship isn't painted as perfect.
When Basil became a bishop, in the middle of a church dispute, he made Gregory bishop of a small town called Sasima. Gregory describes the place as a dusty, noisy crossroads.
He felt used, and he said so to Basil, sharply. By his own telling, he never really took up the post. The friendship was badly strained.
And yet the long speech of praise came from Gregory. He kept the friend, and told the truth about the wound. Fourth, the other Gregory.
Basil had a younger brother, also named Gregory, who became bishop of Nyssa. You heard him a few days ago, joking about bread and theology.
Basil, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus are honored together as the Cappadocian Fathers.
One Gregory, a friend who was like a brother; the other, a brother who became a friend in the faith. And two of them, as tomorrow will show, owed a great deal to their older sister.

how: The Catholic Church keeps the memorial of Saints Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen together on one day, honoring the two friends side by side.

games.q: what does “two gregorys and a friendship” mean?
o: two popes named Gregory who wrote to each other
Basil's friend from Athens, and Basil's own brother
two desert monks who shared one cell for years

games.q: two Gregorys and a friendship — tap the pairs.
p: the town that strained the friendship
to the churches and to lessons

s: the two Gregorys are the same man
Gregory of Nazianzus was Basil's friend; Gregory of Nyssa was Basil's brother.
Basil and Gregory's friendship never had a quarrel
Basil made Gregory bishop of Sasima, and Gregory felt used and told him so.
Gregory gave a long speech in Basil's honor after he died
and it's where we hear about Athens and one soul in two bodies.

games.q: you're Gregory. your best friend, now a bishop, names you bishop of a dusty crossroads town. what do you do?
o: move there gladly and thank him.
protest sharply, and never really take up the post.
games.why: Gregory complained bitterly and, by his own telling, never really served at Sasima. but the friendship held, and he gave the speech in Basil's honor.

practice: Let a face come to mind, someone who shared a room or a road or a hard year with you, whether you're still close or life pulled you apart.
Remember one thing they gave you, a favor, a laugh, a word at the right time, and stay with it. If you pray, thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Two Gregorys and a friendship. Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil's friend since Athens, and Gregory of Nyssa, Basil's brother. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: friendship — the bond Gregory describes between himself and Basil.

carryVoice: Your line: one soul in two bodies. Even a strained friendship can be kept. Day seven hundred twenty-six.
